entry_comparison_index.title: When too much turns bitter
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The useful action—extracting juice—becomes counterproductive when carried too far. The warning is about proportion: pressing for one more favour, one more concession or one more advantage may damage what was already achieved. It does not mean that effort itself is bad.
entry_comparison_index.context: The image makes a social judgement through an ordinary kitchen action. This reading explains the metaphor; it is not a scientific claim about every citrus fruit or a documented account of how the proverb originated.

entry_comparison_index.title: Inviting trouble
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker imagines someone summoning the very trouble they could have avoided. Used ironically, it criticises an unnecessary provocation or a knowingly risky decision. It should not be used to blame someone for harm they did not choose.
entry_comparison_index.context: ବଳଦ is rendered here as ox or bullock. The horned animal supplies the force of the image; the wording alone cannot establish a particular village, farming community or date of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: There will be another winter
entry_comparison_index.meaning: One difficult season is not the last occasion on which we may need help. The saying can warn against treating a temporary advantage as permanent, or remind someone who refuses help that circumstances may change. Tone matters: it can sound like practical advice or a pointed warning.
entry_comparison_index.context: Magha supplies the seasonal image. The central point is recurring need and changing fortunes, not a precise forecast or a claim that cold is confined to one calendar month.

entry_comparison_index.title: Learning when responsibility arrives
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Taking responsibility can force a beginner to learn the necessary skill. The compressed wording leaves the instrument unnamed; imagining a carried percussion instrument helps explain the metaphor, but does not establish which instrument first inspired it. This is encouragement to learn through doing, not a guarantee that preparation is unnecessary.
entry_comparison_index.context: The body carrying a burden and the hands learning a performance meet in one image. No historical link to a named musical tradition has been verified.

entry_comparison_index.title: Not even a straw broken
entry_comparison_index.meaning: This expression makes a very small action stand for any contribution at all. Saying that someone has not done even this means they have done no work in the situation being discussed. It is an idiomatic phrase rather than a complete rhymed maxim.
entry_comparison_index.context: Straw provides a small, light object in the verbal image. The comparison with an English idiom explains the sense; it is not a claim of translation, borrowing or shared origin.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କହି ଦେଉଥାଇ ପରକୁ, ବୁଦ୍ଧି ନ ଦିଶଇ ଘରକୁ
entry_comparison_index.title: Advice that stops at the doorstep
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The criticism is the gap between giving advice and practising it. The outward-facing adviser appears wise, yet fails to apply that wisdom to their own affairs. The saying invites self-examination; it does not imply that advice is worthless whenever its giver has difficulties.
entry_comparison_index.context: The rhyme of ପରକୁ and ଘରକୁ reinforces the contrast between others and home. Here the structure is part of the saying’s force, not just decoration.

entry_comparison_index.title: Noise is not the same as action
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The contrast between loud thunder and absent rain is used to question bluster: impressive promises or threats do not necessarily lead to action. Read the sentence figuratively. Thunderstorms can, of course, bring rain; the proverb is not a dependable weather rule.
entry_comparison_index.context: Weather becomes a way of talking about human speech. Similar imagery elsewhere would not by itself prove where this Odia wording originated.

entry_comparison_index.title: Planting when the meal is due
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The joke is a mismatch between a long preparation and an immediate need. Planting a crop when the occasion has arrived cannot supply that occasion’s meal. The saying criticises starting essential work too late, rather than the act of planting itself.
entry_comparison_index.context: The wedding and vegetable crop create the contrast. This does not prove eggplant is required at every Odia wedding or identify a particular community’s menu. The graphic illustrates lead time, not an agricultural timetable.

entry_comparison_index.title: Anger aimed at the bowl
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The unpleasant thing is the medicine, but the anger is directed at its container. The expression describes displaced frustration: attacking a messenger, object or bystander instead of addressing the actual problem.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source writes ଓଷଦ and କାମୁଡିବା; this edition preserves those forms rather than silently replacing them with modern spellings. The image explains behaviour and gives no advice about taking medicine.

entry_comparison_index.title: A little game, an enormous quarrel
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A small disagreement grows into an outsized conflict. The Mahabharata provides a culturally recognisable scale of conflict. The expression is not evidence that the epic war literally began with this named game, and the game’s precise historical rules have not been established here.
entry_comparison_index.context: ଝିମିଟି is retained rather than replaced by an invented modern game. The contrast is between a modest starting point and epic-scale escalation.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅଧର୍ମ ବିତ୍ତ ବଢେ ବହୁତ, ଗଲା ବେଳେ ଯାଏ ମୂଳ ସହିତ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: When dishonest gain takes the roots with it
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image contrasts rapid growth with loss at the root. Wealth obtained dishonestly may look impressive, yet the conduct behind it can endanger the whole household or enterprise. This is a moral warning about how gain is obtained, not a reliable prediction that every dishonest person will become poor.
entry_comparison_index.context: The rhyme of ବହୁତ and ସହିତ gives the warning a memorable close. The root image suggests losing the foundation, not merely the most recent gain. A version appears as the opening proverb of the1893 collection.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆଲୋ ସଖି, ଆପଣା ମହତ ଆପେ ରଖି
entry_comparison_index.title: Keeping one’s own dignity
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The friendly address makes this advice sound like one person speaking directly to another: preserve your dignity through your own conduct. It may counsel restraint when someone is tempted to join a humiliating quarrel or chase approval. It does not make a person responsible for mistreatment inflicted by others.
entry_comparison_index.context: The contemporary witness begins ଆଲୋ ସଖି. The1893 scan appears to begin ଆରେ ସଖି; that difference is retained as a provisional historical reading. The wording does not establish who first used the saying or confine its advice to one gender.

entry_comparison_index.title: When praise becomes suspicious
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Exaggerated displays of devotion or deference can invite suspicion that the speaker wants something. In everyday use the warning can concern flattery, not only religious devotion. The force comes from the deliberately sharp word “thief”; the saying itself is not evidence that a particular admirer is dishonest.
entry_comparison_index.context: ଭକ୍ତି supplies the outward appearance of reverence, while ଚୋର supplies the hidden motive in the proverb’s contrast. Interpretation depends on the conversation; sincere devotion is not being classified as theft.

entry_comparison_index.title: Swinging without seeing
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A stick swung in darkness may miss its intended target because the person cannot see where to aim. The expression describes guesses or effort without adequate information. Its criticism is not that no effort is being made, but that effort has no dependable direction.
entry_comparison_index.context: This is an idiomatic action phrase rather than a complete rhyming couplet. Darkness is the image for missing information; no specific origin incident has been established.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅରଜି ନପାରେ ମୁଣ୍ଡ, ସୁଆଦ ଲୋଡୁଚି ତୁଣ୍ଡ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: An appetite larger than the means
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The line sets the head’s inability to earn against the mouth’s demand for tasty food. It can rebuke expectations of luxury that do not match available means or contribution. Its tone is sharp and can be hurtful when applied to someone whose circumstances are outside their control.
entry_comparison_index.context: ମୁଣ୍ଡ and ତୁଣ୍ଡ create a compact rhyme between earning and appetite. A possible related line in the1893 scan remains unverified; its uncertain wording is not presented here as a confirmed historical match.

entry_comparison_index.title: When means are short
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The line connects limited means with the distress of being unable to meet needs. Its compact rhyme can express sympathy for someone trying to make a small sum cover many demands. It need not be read as an accusation of greed or a judgement about character.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source adds an explanation about being unable to obtain necessities. That explanatory parenthesis is kept outside the saying itself.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆଜି କୁରୁ କୁରୁ ହସୁ, କାଲି ଲଙ୍ଗଳ କାହିଁରେ ଚଷୁ ?
entry_comparison_index.title: Spending tomorrow’s means today
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The teasing question asks what will remain after today’s enjoyment. It warns against consuming the very means needed for tomorrow’s work. The pleasure is immediate, while the cost becomes visible only when work must resume.
entry_comparison_index.context: The digital witness supplies a story of burning a plough as feast fuel. Treat that as its illustration of the saying, not a verified event or origin. Its citation currently displays a script error.

entry_comparison_index.title: Responding to the occasion
entry_comparison_index.meaning: This compressed expression advises a fitting response to the circumstances. It may interrupt someone who insists on handling every situation in the same way. The point is practical judgement about this occasion, rather than a rule that commitments can always be discarded.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source itself supplies an English gloss about appropriate action. The elliptical Odia is retained; the English rendering makes the implied advice explicit.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆସିଲ ବନ୍ଧୁ ଭଲ କଲ, ବସିବାକୁ ନାହିଁ ଠା, ଯେଉଁ ବାଟେ ବାଟେ ଆସିଲ ବନ୍ଧୁ ସେଇ ବାଟେ ବାଟେ ଯା ।
entry_comparison_index.title: A welcome that sends you away
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The opening sounds hospitable, but the ending cancels the welcome. The humour lies in that sudden reversal: someone offers warm words while making it plain that the visitor is unwanted. Used pointedly, it exposes courtesy that provides no actual welcome.
entry_comparison_index.context: The repeated address to a friend sharpens the irony. The example extends that verbal pattern to another setting; no historical hospitality custom is being asserted.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କାଚ, କାଚ, ମଣି, ମଣି, କିଣା ବିକା ବେଳେ ଜଣା ଜଣି
entry_comparison_index.title: Value put to the test
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Resemblance and confident claims are not enough to establish value. The saying imagines a transaction as the moment when differences become consequential. It can be used when an attractive promise finally has to face a practical test.
entry_comparison_index.context: The image comes from comparing valuable objects with lookalikes. It is a metaphor about testing claims, not a guarantee that markets always recognise quality.

entry_comparison_index.title: Making a small irritation worse
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An action that brings brief relief can deepen the original trouble. In conversation, the expression can describe reopening a minor grievance until it becomes a serious quarrel. The rebuke is directed at aggravating the problem rather than resolving it.
entry_comparison_index.context: The bodily image supplies a social metaphor. This entry explains that metaphor and offers no medical advice.

entry_comparison_index.title: Getting ahead of the occasion
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image mocks preparation that runs ahead of any confirmed need. Someone has acted as though the next step were certain before checking whether the situation calls for it. The saying is sharper than a general reminder to plan carefully.
entry_comparison_index.context: The river and undressing belong to the saying’s literal scene. They do not establish a particular place, journey or bathing custom as its origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Plans are still untested
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An advance plan may look settled until circumstances put it to the test. The source explains the line as a warning that earlier arrangements can fall apart at the appointed time. It tempers certainty without making preparation itself pointless.
entry_comparison_index.context: The digital list numbers the saying12 and its explanation13. Those are one saying with its gloss, not two entries. The raw or unripe image marks something not yet dependable.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମୋତେ ନ ଅଣ୍ଟେ ମୁଁ ନେଇ କରି ସାଇରେ ବାଣ୍ଟେ
entry_comparison_index.title: Giving beyond one’s means
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker describes a mismatch between available means and a display of generosity. It can question a promise to provide for everyone when the giver has not secured enough to do so. Its irony concerns overextension; it need not belittle sharing during hardship.
entry_comparison_index.context: The neighbourhood gives the boast an audience. This is an editorial reading of the recorded wording; the witness supplies no separate explanation for this item.

entry_comparison_index.title: Nodding without understanding
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A person keeps signalling agreement whether or not they understand what is being said. The source’s gloss makes the gap between the nod and comprehension explicit. The expression can tease empty assent or call attention to it when a real decision requires understanding.
entry_comparison_index.context: The animal comparison belongs to the figurative expression. The entry makes no zoological claim about why a lizard moves its head.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଏ ଘର ମାଉସୀ ସେ ଘର ପିଉସୀ
entry_comparison_index.title: Making oneself welcome on every side
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The expression portrays someone claiming closeness everywhere while carrying damaging talk between people. The source gloss stresses pleasing both sides and creating discord. Its target is manipulative familiarity, not genuine friendship across households.
entry_comparison_index.context: ମାଉସୀ and ପିଉସୀ are distinct kinship terms, preserved in the literal rendering. The figurative criticism does not describe a trait of actual aunts or of women generally.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅଜାଗା ଘା ଦେଖି ହୁଏ ନାହିଁ କି ଦେଖାଇ ହୁଏ ନାହିଁ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: A difficulty too awkward to disclose
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image conveys a predicament that is hard to inspect privately and embarrassing to disclose. In conversation, it can express the burden of a trouble someone feels unable to explain openly. Its force lies in that double bind, rather than in a recommendation to keep suffering secret.
entry_comparison_index.context: The bodily image is retained in the literal rendering. The figurative explanation is an editorial reading; no medical claim or origin incident is established.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଅଙ୍ଗୁଳି ସନ୍ଧିରେ ମଳି
ଭିତରେ ଭିତରେ ସଲା ସୁତୁରାଲୋ
ଉପରେ ଉପରେ କଳି ।
entry_comparison_index.title: A quarrel staged for others
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Two sides appear to fight while privately cooperating. The repeated contrast between inside and outside exposes a performance meant to mislead an audience. The saying accuses the quarrel of being staged; it does not merely describe people who disagree but remain friendly.
entry_comparison_index.context: The three source lines are retained. The address particle ଲୋ adds a conversational voice; the English rendering conveys the contrast without inventing a named listener.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଏ କଥା ରହିଲା ମନେ, ବେଳ କାଳ ଦେଖି କହିବି ଦିନେ
entry_comparison_index.title: Saving a reply for later
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker declines an immediate reply while making clear that the matter is not forgotten. Depending on the situation, the line can sound restrained, pointed or quietly threatening. It preserves a future opportunity to answer rather than offering reconciliation now.
entry_comparison_index.context: The time and occasion remain unspecified in the wording. This entry explains its possible conversational tone without assigning it a historical dispute.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କାହାକୁ କହିବା, କପାଳରେ ସିନା କର ମାରିବା
entry_comparison_index.title: Who is there to tell?
entry_comparison_index.meaning: This is a gesture of exasperation put into words. The speaker feels that complaining will find no useful listener, so frustration turns into a weary reaction. It may be rueful or comic; it expresses a feeling of helplessness without proving that help is unavailable.
entry_comparison_index.context: କର means hand here. The literal gesture helps convey the expression; no physical action is prescribed by the explanation.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମୋତେ ଯେତେ ମାଠିବୁ ମାଠ ମୁହିଁ ସେଇ ଦରପଡ଼ା କାଠ
entry_comparison_index.title: Refusing to be polished into something else
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker declares that repeated efforts to change or improve them will not work. The blunt material image can make the refusal comic, defiant or self-deprecating. It voices a stance in a conversation, not a truth that people cannot learn or change.
entry_comparison_index.context: The wood image and the first-person voice are preserved. This is distinct from enduring pressure: here the emphasis falls on resisting another person’s attempts to remake the speaker. The source spells the word ଦରପଡ଼ା. “Half-burnt” is an editorial interpretation of that spelling, not a verified correction to the original; lexical and human review remain pending.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ତୁ କେତେ ହଲଉଚୁ ହଲା...
ମୁଁ କିଛି ନହଲିଲେ ଗଲା...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: You can shake; I need not move
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker answers pressure with a challenge. Another person may keep trying to unsettle them, but the speaker claims control over their own response. The tone can convey resolve or stubbornness; its value depends on what they are refusing to yield about.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source introduces these lines as a response by someone determined. That introductory gloss is excluded from the headword. The digital ellipses and exclamation marks are retained, not claimed as ancient punctuation.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ମାଲୋ ମଲି,
ଗାଁ ଚାରିଆଡ଼େ ବୁଲି ଆଇଲି...
କେହି ନକହିଲେ ବସ ବୋଲି...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: No one even asked me to sit
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The complaint turns a small invitation into the measure of being welcomed. After going everywhere, the speaker has not received even that acknowledgement. The exaggerated opening can make the hurt comic, while the last line reveals the modest courtesy that was missing.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source places it under a gloss about not receiving due respect. The dramatic ମଲି is rendered as an exclamation, not a report of death. No universal village hospitality rule is inferred.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
କ୍ଷୀର ଉତୁରିଲେ ଚୁଲିକୁ,
ମଣିଷ ଉତୁରିଲେ ଗାତକୁ...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: Pride that boils over
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The first line supplies an everyday overflow; the second turns it into a warning about arrogance. The source explicitly frames the saying as a response to excessive pride. Its sharp downward ending suggests that losing restraint can bring a fall.
entry_comparison_index.context: The comparison is between two kinds of overstepping. It is a figurative warning, not a prediction that every proud person will suffer a particular fate. The source’s digital punctuation is preserved.

entry_comparison_index.title: Early signs
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The small plant provides an image for qualities becoming noticeable early. Someone may use the saying when a beginner already shows promise. Early signs can be encouraging without fixing what a child or learner must become.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places this clause beside a contrasting plant comparison. Only the tulasi clause is displayed here. This is a figurative reading, not a botanical test or a claim about inherited ability.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ନାହିଁ ମାମୁଁ ଠଉଁ କଣା ମାମୁ ଭଲ
entry_comparison_index.title: Some help rather than none
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The comparison expresses a preference for an imperfect resource over having none. Its family image assumes that an uncle can offer care or assistance. The point can be explained without treating disability as a measure of a person’s worth.
entry_comparison_index.context: The historical-style dictionary explanation connects the maternal uncle with care for a nephew. The disability language is preserved as documented wording and identified as a dated comparison; no universal family practice is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.title: A hiding place that gives you away
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Someone’s attempt to conceal a matter leaves an obvious clue. The question punctures the pretence of secrecy: what is meant to be hidden is still visible. It can tease a transparent excuse without proving any particular accusation.
entry_comparison_index.context: The licensed page gives this as an additional expression beneath another saying. It is recorded here in its own wording; the neighbouring saying and its gloss are not treated as identical.

entry_comparison_index.title: Learning from a lost support
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Losing something relied upon can make a person more careful afterwards. The saying compresses that lesson into the loss of a walking stick. It is a figurative warning about repeating mistakes, not a factual assertion about blind people or a guarantee that a loss happens only once.
entry_comparison_index.context: The wording uses blindness and a stick as an image of dependence on a support. Explain the image without reducing blind people to helplessness or using it to mock disability.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆପଣା ହସ୍ତେ ଜିହ୍ଵା ଛେଦି, କେ ଅଛି ତାର ପ୍ରତିବାଦୀ
entry_comparison_index.title: A difficulty caused by one’s own act
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The sharp image points to trouble brought about by one’s own action. It challenges an attempt to shift responsibility elsewhere. It should not be used to assume that every hardship is self-caused or that someone who made a mistake no longer deserves help.
entry_comparison_index.context: The bodily injury is a rhetorical image, not an instruction. The final question is rendered as a challenge to protest; it is not evidence for a historical incident.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆରେ ଢମଣା , ବୁଲି ବୁଲିକରି ସେଇ ଅଗଣା ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Back to the same courtyard
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A wandering journey ends where it began. In conversation, the image can describe repeated detours that bring no change, or someone returning to a familiar place after trying alternatives. The tone may be teasing or critical, depending on the situation.
entry_comparison_index.context: The creature-name dhamana is retained without assigning a precise species. The courtyard supplies the image of return; no belief about animal behaviour or local origin is established.

entry_comparison_index.title: Work that does not move forward
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image suggests effort whose result is undone as the work proceeds. It can be used for a task that stays unfinished because each advance is cancelled by another action. Its bodily caricature should be recognized rather than turned into a judgment about disabled people.
entry_comparison_index.context: Godara is rendered as the saying’s description of swollen legs, without diagnosing a medical condition. The interpretation concerns self-defeating work, not physical capacity or personal worth. The figurative explanation is an editorial interpretation, not a separately verified traditional gloss.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମୁଳୁରୁ ମାଇପ ନାହିଁ ପୁଅ ନାଁ ଗୋପାଳ
entry_comparison_index.title: Naming the child before the family exists
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Plans have moved ahead of the conditions needed to carry them out. The family scene makes the missing first step conspicuous: a later detail has been settled while the basic situation is still imaginary. It can mock premature certainty rather than planning itself.
entry_comparison_index.context: The wording uses a blunt term for wife and a familiar personal name. It documents a domestic image, not a rule about marriage, parenthood or a person’s entitlement to either.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଠାକୁର ଘରେ କିଏ ରେ? ନାଁ ମୁଁ କଦଳୀ ଖାଇନାହିଁ
entry_comparison_index.title: An answer that reveals too much
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The question asks who is there, but the answer denies an act nobody mentioned. That unsolicited detail directs attention to the speaker’s possible concern. The humour comes from the mismatch between question and reply; a defensive answer alone does not establish guilt.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary quotes this dialogue under the connective use of na and explicitly calls it a dhaga. The shrine room and bananas belong to the saying; no actual theft, temple custom or origin story is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଘଇତା ପଛେ ମରୁ କିନ୍ତୁ ସଉତୁଣି ରାଣ୍ଡ ହେଉ!.
entry_comparison_index.title: Resentment that harms oneself
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Spite becomes so strong that the speaker accepts a shared loss merely to hurt a rival. The deliberately harsh domestic scene exposes the cost of that desire. It is a criticism of destructive resentment, not a claim that women or co-wives naturally behave this way.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source preserves a coarse term for widow and a co-wife rivalry image. Those gendered insults are part of the documented wording, not language the explanation endorses or a history of any particular household. The figurative explanation is an editorial interpretation, not a separately verified traditional gloss.

entry_comparison_index.title: Familiarity that hides someone’s worth
entry_comparison_index.meaning: People who have known someone from everyday village life may dismiss that person instead of recognizing their qualities. The belittling description makes that dismissiveness audible. The saying can challenge a narrow local judgment without endorsing the insult directed at the bride.
entry_comparison_index.context: The literal image is gendered and dismissive. The editorial reading concerns undervaluing the familiar; neither a universal village custom nor the saying’s first historical use is known.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କଂସାରୀ ଘର ପାରାଙ୍କୁ କୁଲା ଢାଉଁ ଢାଉଁ
entry_comparison_index.title: A noise that does not impress
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An attempt to startle or impress has little effect on someone already accustomed to the disturbance. The joke contrasts the small display of noise with the noisy workshop imagined around the birds. It can describe an empty threat made to an experienced listener.
entry_comparison_index.context: The workshop and winnowing tray form the saying’s acoustic image. Kansari is translated through the craft role in this expression; it does not establish the identity of any present maker or an inherited community trait.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆଲୋ ମୁତୁରି ଶୋଇବା, ତୁ ମୁତୁରୀ କି ମୁଁ ମୁତୁରା ହେଂସ କାହିଁପାଇଁ ଧୋଇବା...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: Both share the fault
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The licensed page places this crude joke in the situation of two people sharing the same fault. One possible reading is that their shared embarrassment lets both excuse leaving things as they are. The specific suggestion of mutual indulgence is an editorial interpretation; the witness does not supply a detailed explanation. This bodily image should not be used to shame someone with an actual condition.
entry_comparison_index.context: The licensed witness has a substantially different word order from the discovery list. Its bodily and gendered forms are retained without smoothing them into that other version. Bed-wetting is a comic image here, not a moral judgment about an actual condition. The figurative explanation is an editorial interpretation, not a separately verified traditional gloss.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଢିଙ୍କି ସ୍ୱର୍ଗକୁ ଗଲେ ବି ଧାନ କୁଟିବ
entry_comparison_index.title: The same work, even in heaven
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The joke gives a rice-pounding implement a grand change of address but leaves its work exactly as before. In conversation, it can tease someone who brings an old habit into a new setting, or express frustration that a change of place has changed nothing. The pointed contrast is between heaven and the same everyday task.
entry_comparison_index.context: Dhinki is retained as the name of the traditional rice-pounding implement; paddy is rice still in its husk. Heaven supplies the exaggerated destination. This reading does not turn an implement’s fixed function into a claim that people cannot change, or that anyone must remain in an inherited occupation.

entry_comparison_index.title: Making a small thing enormous
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A tiny seed is imagined as something much larger. The expression calls out exaggeration: a small mistake, slight or difficulty has been enlarged beyond proportion. Its force is a brisk objection to the scale of the telling, rather than a claim that the original problem did not exist.
entry_comparison_index.context: The compact sound-pair ତିଳ and ତାଳ carries the jump in scale. The English rendering takes ତାଳ as the palmyra fruit; the short witness does not spell out that referent, so this lexical choice remains for fluent-reader review. The explanation should not be used to dismiss another person’s distress without understanding it.

entry_comparison_index.title: More oil for an already oiled head
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The extra oil goes where there is already oil. Used socially, the image questions giving still more attention, help or advantage to someone already well provided for, while others go without. It can sound wry or resentful, depending on who is speaking and how the benefit is being distributed.
entry_comparison_index.context: The head and oil remain the material image; no named oiling ritual, caste practice or historical incident is implied. The emphasis here is advantage being added to advantage. Other conversational uses, including praise directed at powerful people, need their own context rather than being treated as the only meaning.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆଜ ହୁଁ ଏଡ଼େ, ପାଣି ପଡିଲେ ହବୁ କେଡ଼େ
entry_comparison_index.title: A warning before things grow worse
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An early fault prompts a warning about what unchecked growth could bring. It criticises present behaviour, not a child’s unchangeable nature.
entry_comparison_index.context: The water-and-growth image is figurative. The source presents this as a negative warning.

entry_comparison_index.title: Complaining while collecting
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The complaint continues while the benefits are quietly gathered. Read as irony about dissatisfaction that does not prevent acceptance.
entry_comparison_index.context: Tying things into a bundle supplies the image. This interpretation is editorial; the witness provides no gloss.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଗଙ୍ଗା ବୋଇଲେ ଥିବି ଗାଙ୍ଗୀ ବୋଇଲେ ଯିବି
entry_comparison_index.title: The name makes the difference
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A change in address changes the reception. The contrast can tease someone who insists on a particular form of respect.
entry_comparison_index.context: Ganga and Gangi are retained as names; no real woman or originating incident is identified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ସେଇ ଘଇତା କଲୁ, ବୟସ ଗଡ଼େଇ ଦେଲୁ!
entry_comparison_index.title: The same choice after all that delay
entry_comparison_index.meaning: After prolonged delay, the eventual choice is the one available before. The jibe targets the wasted interval.
entry_comparison_index.context: Marriage supplies the wording. It need not be used to pressure anyone into marrying early.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ତୁଛାକୁ ଏତେ ନା ମୁଦି ନାହିଁ ଗୋଡ଼ କଛାଡୁ କେତେ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: All that stamping over nothing
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An exaggerated display outruns what there is to display. The source gloss connects it with being agitated over nothing.
entry_comparison_index.context: The witness does not specify the ring’s position or supply a story behind the image.

entry_comparison_index.title: Following another into a mistake
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Someone follows another’s lead into a mistake. The animal scene makes imitation look foolish.
entry_comparison_index.context: Animal names are general renderings, not precise species identifications or claims about animal behaviour.

entry_comparison_index.title: Wisdom in consultation
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The religious image gives weight to people deliberating together. It can encourage consultation rather than a decision made alone; it does not guarantee a group is right.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places this under five people gathered to discuss a subject. It is not the differently worded source127 position15.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଚୋର ମା ଯଦି କାନ୍ଦେ ଆଖି ମଳିମଳି କାନ୍ଦେ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Tears that conceal support
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source reads the display of distress as concealed support for a wrongdoer. The charge is complicity behind appearances, not proof that a crying relative is guilty.
entry_comparison_index.context: The maternal figure belongs to the saying; responsibility cannot be inferred from kinship or tears alone.

entry_comparison_index.title: Taken while you watched
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A shrewd person gains the advantage while someone else watches helplessly. The bite lies in noticing the trick too late.
entry_comparison_index.context: Mahapatra is retained from the wording, not treated as evidence about a surname or community.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅଲାଜୁକ ଷାଠିଆ ପାନ ନାହିଁ ଗୁଆ ନାହିଁ ଖାଲି ବଟୁଆ!
entry_comparison_index.title: An impressive pouch with nothing inside
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The accessory promises substance that is absent. The source gloss identifies shameless outward boasting.
entry_comparison_index.context: The betel pouch supplies the contrast. “Show-off” renders the source’s overall sense; the colloquial opening is not independently glossed word by word.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କୁହାଯାଉଥାଇ ସିନା, ତୁହାଇ ତୁହାଇ ପୁଟ ଦେଲେ କାହିଁ, ଲୁହା କି ହୋଇବ ସୁନା
entry_comparison_index.title: The wrong process cannot make gold
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Repeating a process does not ensure the transformation wanted. This editorial reading questions an unsuitable method, not anyone’s capacity to learn.
entry_comparison_index.context: A metalworking image, not a claim of innate human rank or an instruction for processing metals.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଭାସି ଯାଉଥିଲୁ ମଝିନଇରେ ଧରି ଆଣିଥିଲି ତତେ, ଠାକୁଆ ଗାଲରେ ମାଉଁଶ ଲାଗିଲା ଜବାବ ଦେଉଛୁ ମତେ
entry_comparison_index.title: Remembering a rescue
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker resents defiance from someone previously helped. The rescue creates the contrast between former dependence and present confidence.
entry_comparison_index.context: Editorial interpretation of an unglossed witness. Receiving help does not remove a person’s right to disagree.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ରାଧା କହିଲେ ଦୂତୀ କି, ଯାହା ହେଇଚି ସେତିକି...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: What has happened has happened
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A resigned response when events have become difficult to contain: further words cannot undo what has occurred.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source invokes Radha and a female messenger but names no underlying poem or episode; none is supplied here.

entry_comparison_index.title: A witness with a stake in the story
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The supposed witness has a connection to the person being defended. The pointed question is whether that testimony is independent.
entry_comparison_index.context: The occupational caricature is not evidence about any community’s honesty. Shared interests invite scrutiny, not automatic disbelief.

entry_comparison_index.title: Running only to the familiar bush
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source uses the short dash to mock a narrow range of thought. Much motion may still lead only to a familiar answer.
entry_comparison_index.context: Siju is retained as the plant name. This is a figurative reading, not a zoological claim or a judgment of fixed intelligence.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କାଣୀ ବିରାଡ଼ି କୁଜି ଅସରପା ଉପରେ ରଜା
entry_comparison_index.title: Power over someone weaker
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Even a limited power can dominate a weaker opponent. The contrast makes that small kingdom look less impressive.
entry_comparison_index.context: Editorial reading: the source gloss repeats the line. Its bodily caricatures are retained for documentation, not endorsed as measures of human worth.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅଖ ବୁଲୁଥିଲେ ଚକ ବୁଲୁଥାଏ, ବୁଲି ପଡୁଥାଏ ମହି, ସଂସାର ଭିତରେ ଘର କରିଥିଲେ ପଥର ପଡ଼ିଲେ ସହି ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Living with the jolts
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The movement of ordinary life leads into counsel to withstand hardship. Endurance is the proposed response to unavoidable jolts.
entry_comparison_index.context: Editorial interpretation of an unglossed verse. Endurance does not require accepting abuse or preventable harm.

entry_comparison_index.title: Look at your own feet
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A sharp retort turns scrutiny back on the critic: examine your own shortcomings before mocking someone else’s.
entry_comparison_index.context: The body-directed insult is part of the historical-style wording, not a recommended way to address illness or disability. Meaning is an editorial reading.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଗଂଗାଦି ନାନା ତୀର୍ଥ ନିକଟେ ଥାଇଣ ଚାତକ, ଜଳଦ ଜଳ ଟୋପେକୁ ଆଶ୍ରାକରି ଅବିରତେ ତୃଷୀକ
entry_comparison_index.title: Waiting for one particular drop
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse pictures longing fixed on one source despite alternatives nearby. It may evoke steadfast desire; context determines whether that seems admirable or impractical.
entry_comparison_index.context: Read as a literary bird-image, not a claim about a species’ drinking habits. The page names no author or originating work.

entry_comparison_index.title: The catch and the meal differ
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The contrast suggests that producing something does not ensure enjoying it oneself. The line can point to a gap between someone’s work and their own circumstances.
entry_comparison_index.context: Editorial reading of an unglossed line. Keuta is retained from the witness; this is not evidence about a community’s diet, poverty or food preferences.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମାଗି ଖାଉଥାଏ ବାସି ତୋଡ଼ାଣି, ଯାଚିଲେ ନ ଖାଏ ସର ଲବଣୀ
entry_comparison_index.title: Refusing what is freely offered
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The contrast mocks a refusal that appears at odds with what someone usually seeks. An unsolicited offer is rejected despite being presented as more desirable.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary explicitly labels this a dhaga under offering something. Rice-water interprets the witness spelling ତୋଡ଼ାଣି without changing it. The saying does not explain why the offer is refused; consent and personal preference remain valid.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଛାଡ଼ ଅଞ୍ଚଳ ମହାବାହୁ...
ଏ ଜନ୍ମେ ଭେଟ ନାହିଁ ଆଉ...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: A dramatic farewell
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source places this farewell under distress that feels unbearable. Its absolute language gives the parting a dramatic finality.
entry_comparison_index.context: The witness names no underlying song or episode. Mahabahu is rendered literally; no particular speaker or deity is assigned.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ବଣ ପୋଡ଼ିଲେ ଦୁନିଆ ଜାଣେ, ମନ ପୋଡ଼ିଲେ କେହୀ ନ ଜାଣେ
entry_comparison_index.title: The fire nobody sees
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Visible calamity draws attention; private grief can remain unnoticed. The contrast asks the listener to recognise pain that has no outward blaze.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places this under mental distress. “No one” is the saying’s emphatic contrast, not a claim that support is impossible.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଚଷା ହୁଡ଼ିଲେ ବରଷେ, ମଣିଷ ହୁଡିଲେ ପୁରୁଷେ
entry_comparison_index.title: A year lost and a life affected
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A seasonal mistake is contrasted with a decision that can shape a life. The warning concerns the scale of consequences, not the impossibility of recovery.
entry_comparison_index.context: The cited sense defines ପୁରୁଷ as lifetime, not generation. ଚଷା is read in the farming image; no caste-wide trait is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.title: No rare treat for a prince
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Something impressive to one person may be ordinary to someone with easy access. The rhetorical question puts the proposed treat in perspective.
entry_comparison_index.context: Khaja remains the named sweet. The source gloss explains ready access; no particular prince or court incident is identified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ରଜାର ପ୍ରଜା ନୁହେଁ କି ସାହୁର ଖାତକ ନୁହେଁ
entry_comparison_index.title: Beholden to neither
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker presents themself as independent and free of debt. It is a forceful refusal to be treated as someone under another’s control.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary gloss supports independence and absence of debt. This is figurative self-assertion, not a legal exemption from obligations.

entry_comparison_index.title: Authority without judgment
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A curt, rhyming criticism of a ruler’s awkward understanding. Authority has not brought good judgment.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary gloss supplies the sense. This is a proverbial taunt, not a claim about all rulers.

entry_comparison_index.title: A straw-bundle adviser
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Poor leadership is compounded by equally foolish advice. The pairing, rather than the ruler alone, is the target.
entry_comparison_index.context: Straw-bundle is a belittling image. The source gloss explicitly describes a foolish adviser to an unjust ruler.

entry_comparison_index.title: Trading alongside a prince
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A person with fewer resources can suffer by joining someone whose means are much greater. The warning concerns an unequal undertaking.
entry_comparison_index.context: This follows the dictionary gloss; it is not a documented trading incident or a rule against friendships across income levels.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଘର ଦେଖି ଦେଇ କି, ବର ଦେଖି ଦେଇ
entry_comparison_index.title: The household or the groom?
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The question contrasts a family’s standing with the individual being considered for marriage. It exposes two different ways of judging a match.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places ଘର under high family. That records a status-conscious setting, not an endorsement of inherited rank; the saying does not establish either person’s consent.

entry_comparison_index.title: When cold becomes a tiger
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The tiger makes the cold feel fierce.
entry_comparison_index.context: A vivid seasonal image, not a weather forecast.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମାଘେ ଶୀତ, ମେଘେ ଶୀତ, ଯତ୍ର ବାତ ତତ୍ର ଶୀତ
entry_comparison_index.title: Where the cold is felt
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A rhythmic reply names occasions when cold is felt.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary presents it as a reply. Its Sanskrit phrasing is retained; it is not a universal weather rule.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କହି ଜାଣିଲେ କଥା ସୁନ୍ଦର ବାନ୍ଧି ଜାଣିଲେ ମଥା ସୁନ୍ଦର
entry_comparison_index.title: The art of saying it well
entry_comparison_index.meaning: How something is done matters. Well-chosen words are compared with hair arranged by a practised hand.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places this under arranging hair and labels it ଢଗ. The comparison concerns skill, not a rule about personal appearance.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅଳପ ନିଦକୁ ବହୁତ କଥା, ଝୁରିମରିବାକୁ କଲା ବିଧାତା
entry_comparison_index.title: Little rest, many troubles
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A weary complaint that troubles leave little rest. The exaggerated lament carries the feeling of being overwhelmed.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary cites this under happening/event. This is an editorial reading of its lament, not sleep advice.

entry_comparison_index.title: A meal ends; its reputation remains
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A brief occasion can leave a lasting impression, good or bad. Its memory outlasts the meal.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places କଥା here under fame or notoriety and labels the saying ପ୍ରବଚନ. No particular feast is identified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କଥାର ମଞ୍ଜି, କୁଆ ଧାନ ଖାଏ ବୋହୁକୁ ଗଞ୍ଜି
entry_comparison_index.title: The crow eats; someone else is blamed
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Blame falls on someone other than the one responsible. The contrast exposes how unfair that is.
entry_comparison_index.context: The household scene names a daughter-in-law as the target of blame. It is not a claim about every family or an endorsement of blaming women.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କଥା କହୁଥାଏ କେଉଁ ରସରେ, ମୋତେ ଲାଗୁଥାଏ ପରିହାସରେ
entry_comparison_index.title: That sounds like mockery to me
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A listener hears ridicule, whatever the speaker intended. The contrast draws attention to how words are received.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary gives this under manner and a related wording under intention. No particular speaker or quarrel is identified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମାରି ମାରି ଗଲା କାଳକ ଆଉ ରହିଗଲା ଫାଳକ
entry_comparison_index.title: Time slips away
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Time has passed while one was merely getting through it. The remaining half is a rhyming image, not a measured lifespan.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places this under whiling away time. It does not establish the speaker’s age.

entry_comparison_index.title: A threat against someone’s food
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The threat is to deprive someone of food or support rather than strike them. It exposes another form of coercion.
entry_comparison_index.context: Recorded as a saying, not advice or justification for deprivation.

entry_comparison_index.title: Punishing one to warn another
entry_comparison_index.meaning: One person is punished so that someone else takes the warning. The indirect target is the point of the saying.
entry_comparison_index.context: The household image contains violence against women. Recording it does not endorse that violence or claim every family behaves this way.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମୂଳୁଁ ମାଇଲେ ଯିବ ସରି, ଦେବଙ୍କ ସଙ୍ଗେ କିପାଁ କଳି
entry_comparison_index.title: Deal with the root
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The words contrast ending something at its source with quarrelling. Reading this as a call to address the underlying cause is editorial.
entry_comparison_index.context: No originating tale or specific sacred tree is supplied by this dictionary passage. The example does not advocate destruction.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଦେଖିଲେ କଥା ନ କହେ, ନ ଦେଖିଲେ ପାଣି ନ ପିଏ
entry_comparison_index.title: Silent together, restless apart
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The contradiction is the joke: someone seems distant in person but cannot settle when the other is absent.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source labels this ଢଗ under meeting. It names no relationship or reason for the silence.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ହାଟକୁ ଗଲେ କନ୍ୟା ଦେଖିବି ବାଇଗଣ ବିକିବି ଦି କାମ କରିବି
entry_comparison_index.title: Two errands on one trip
entry_comparison_index.meaning: One outing is made to serve two purposes. The unexpected pairing gives the plan its humour.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary places this under seeking. It does not establish a marriage custom or imply buying a bride.

entry_comparison_index.title: From scarcity into famine
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A change meant to escape difficulty leads into something worse. Here କାନ୍ତାର is the dictionary’s famine sense, not its separate forest sense.
entry_comparison_index.context: The food-scarcity image supplies the comparison; no particular famine or historical event is identified.

entry_comparison_index.title: By whatever means
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The expression describes pursuing a result by every available means. Depending on context, it can suggest determination or a willingness to use unfair methods.
entry_comparison_index.context: This is an adverbial idiom in the dictionary, not a complete narrative proverb or an endorsement of deceit.

entry_comparison_index.title: Feeding one at another’s expense
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image exposes a benefit obtained by making another bear the loss. The explanation follows the contrast between the creature killed and the one nourished.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary labels the expression ପ୍ରବଚନ. Its linked insect and bird entries support the literal image; the social application is editorial.

entry_comparison_index.title: Even river sand runs out
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Even a large store can be exhausted if it is continually used without replenishment. The exaggerated sand image makes the scale of the reserve irrelevant.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source places this under consuming savings without earning. It should not be used to blame people unable to work or to deny their need for support.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଚମବାଇଦ କୋଶେ, ତୁଣ୍ଡ ବାଇଦ ଶହସ୍ର କୋଶ
entry_comparison_index.title: Words travel farther than drums
entry_comparison_index.meaning: News passed from person to person can spread much farther than a sound heard at its source. The contrast is deliberate exaggeration, not a measured claim about distance.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary’s sense1 is a report or rumour carried by word of mouth. The longer witness is retained; the discovery list gives only its latter idea.

entry_comparison_index.title: Measure farther than you step
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Examine more of the situation than the immediate step requires. The proverb recommends deliberation before acting; careful preparation can reduce risk without guaranteeing safety.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary itself explains the longer measure and shorter step. These are traditional body-based measures; no fixed modern conversion is needed here.

entry_comparison_index.title: Harm from what was kept close
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Something or someone trusted and kept close becomes the source of harm. The dictionary puts the saying beside its figurative sense of cheating.
entry_comparison_index.context: Violent imagery describes betrayal; it is not an instruction to harm anyone. The source does not establish a particular origin story.

entry_comparison_index.title: Do not delay a good beginning
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Once a worthwhile action is decided, avoid needless delay. This is encouragement to begin, not a reason to abandon judgment or preparation.
entry_comparison_index.context: The Odia dictionary explicitly labels this a Sanskrit proverb. It is included as an expression used in Odia, not claimed as uniquely Odia in origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: A pious appearance that deceives
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A show of devotion conceals conduct that contradicts it. The target is the mismatch between appearance and action, not believers as a group.
entry_comparison_index.context: The exact dictionary spelling ବଇଷମ is preserved. It is given as a figurative synonym under ଭେଖଧାରୀ ବୈଷ୍ଣବ; no animal fable or historical founder is supplied.

entry_comparison_index.title: Each place has its own ways
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A way of doing things that feels ordinary in one place may differ elsewhere. The river image makes local variation easy to picture. The saying invites attention to the place you are in, without declaring every local practice beyond question.
entry_comparison_index.context: The example appears under locality in the dictionary. A separate lexical entry gives particular and differing customs among the senses of ଫାଙ୍କ; that supports the reading used here.

entry_comparison_index.title: One hand cannot clap
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Some things require a response or a shared effort. The image of two palms meeting makes that dependence immediate. It can invite cooperation; it should not be used to assume that both sides bear equal blame for harm.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary explicitly labels this example a dhaga under clapping. The explanation here is editorial, not a recorded account of its first use.

entry_comparison_index.title: What is past cannot be undone
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The maxim urges someone to stop dwelling on an irreversible event and attend to what can still be done. It need not mean forgetting lessons or dismissing grief.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary explicitly labels this a Sanskrit proverb recorded in Odia. It is not a rule about how long someone should grieve.

entry_comparison_index.title: A flower growing in the sky
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An attractive idea has no basis in reality, like a flower imagined as growing in empty sky. The expression questions feasibility rather than imagination itself.
entry_comparison_index.context: This is a figurative compound, listed as a synonym under ଖପୁଷ୍ପ. The dictionary establishes the image, not a uniquely Odia origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: A small search uncovers something larger
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An ordinary investigation unexpectedly brings a much larger matter to light. This explanation follows the contrast in scale; the dictionary does not provide an origin tale.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source labels it ଢଗ under appearing or becoming visible. Mahadeva is Shiva; no particular excavated shrine, village or historical discovery is verified.

entry_comparison_index.title: When silence is read as agreement
entry_comparison_index.meaning: This maxim describes an inference people make from another person’s silence. Silence can also mean hesitation, fear or uncertainty, so it does not establish that someone has agreed.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary identifies a Sanskrit maxim. It is documented here as an expression to examine, not permission to treat silence as consent.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଦୂର ପର୍ବତ ସୁନ୍ଦର; ଦୂର ବନ୍ଧୁ ସୁନ୍ଦର
entry_comparison_index.title: Distance makes things look better
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Distance can hide the rough edges of a place or a relationship. What looks inviting from afar may feel different when we know its everyday difficulties. The saying gently questions an ideal picture; it does not claim that friendship needs distance.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary gives two parallel images: a mountain seen from afar and a friend kept at a distance. This explanation is an editorial reading of that contrast, not an origin story.

entry_comparison_index.title: Giving someone a rough reception
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The ordinary words suggest grades of quality, but together they can describe harsh treatment. In the dictionary’s example, the speaker sends someone away after giving them blows and abuse. The expression conveys that rough reception; reading the words as praise would miss the point. The source records the usage, not a recommendation to treat anyone this way.
entry_comparison_index.context: This is an idiomatic expression documented within a dictionary example, rather than a complete proverbial sentence. The entry heading uses an editorial infinitive for easy lookup. The witness retains the sentence’s actual inflected wording and the dictionary’s explanation. No claim is made about when or where the expression began.

entry_comparison_index.title: An unexpected opening
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Something previously out of reach becomes available by chance. The cat benefits from a broken hanging food sling, rather than from a plan of its own.
entry_comparison_index.context: ଶିକା denotes a rope support for suspended vessels; its separate dictionary entry explains this comparison.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କପାଳେ ନ ଥିଲେ ଭୂପାଳେ ନ ଦିଅନ୍ତି
entry_comparison_index.title: Beyond a ruler’s favour
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The saying voices resignation when hoped-for help fails. It expresses a belief about fate, not proof that effort or assistance is useless.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source places this under the fate sense of କପାଳ.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମୋତେ ମାରନାଁ ମୁଁ ମଲିଣି, ଦୀପ ଲଗେଇ ଦେଖ୍ ପିଠି, ଲାଉ ଚୋର ଭାବ ପାଇଲିଣି
entry_comparison_index.title: Already humiliated
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The dictionary uses this under humiliation: punishment and disgrace have already landed. The protest is not permission for further violence.
entry_comparison_index.context: No actual theft or punishment incident is verified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆମ୍ୱ ଗଛରେ ପାଣି ଦଉଁ ଦଉଁ ଶିମ୍ୱ ଗଛ ମଲା
entry_comparison_index.title: One thing tended, another neglected
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Attention given to one concern can leave another unattended. This is an editorial reading of the contrast, not gardening advice.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary supplies the withering sense; no origin story.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କହିବି ତା ଆଗେ ଶୁଣିବେ କେ? ଘଇତା ଅବୁଝା ମାରିବ ଯେ
entry_comparison_index.title: When speaking feels unsafe
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker fears that a complaint will bring violence instead of a hearing. The saying exposes a situation in which someone feels unheard and unsafe; it does not make that treatment acceptable.
entry_comparison_index.context: ଘଇତା means husband here. The gendered scene belongs to this witness, not a claim about all husbands or households.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଘର ବୁଡ଼ି ପାଣି ଆଣ୍ଠୁଏ ହେଲାଣି ପୁଅଙ୍କର ପିକା ଖିଆ ଛାଡ଼ ଯାଉ ନାହିଁ
entry_comparison_index.title: Habit while the house floods
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image mocks someone who clings to a habit while an urgent problem grows around him. The dictionary marks ପୁଅ here as a satirical reference to a person, not necessarily a child.
entry_comparison_index.context: The separate ପିକା entry identifies a cheroot. No smoking practice is recommended.

entry_comparison_index.title: A hare’s horn
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The expression names something impossible or unreal. Its force comes from looking for a feature the animal does not possess.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary explicitly explains figurative use and lists related impossible images. It is semantically related to existing ଆକାଶକୁସୁମ, but has a distinct image and wording.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଆପଣା ଭଉଣୀ ନ ପାଏ ଭାତଗୁଣ୍ଡା
ଶଳାଶାଳୀ ପାଇଁ ଥୁଆ କ୍ଷୀରମଣ୍ଡା ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Favouring one side of the family
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The contrast criticises conspicuous favour for one set of relatives while someone close goes without. It questions unequal care, not the worth of either relationship.
entry_comparison_index.context: The food contrast is imagery; no universal household custom is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଇଛା ଥିଲେ ଉପାୟ ବଳେ ବଳେ ଆସେ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Finding a way
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Determination can encourage someone to search for a workable approach. The saying offers encouragement, not a guarantee that desire removes every obstacle.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଯେ ଦେଶ ଯାଇ,
ସେ ଫଳ ଖାଇ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Learning to adapt
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The food image invites a visitor to adjust to the place they enter. Adaptation need not mean abandoning personal boundaries or accepting harm.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Acknowledging no authority
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The named divine figures heighten the idea of someone who refuses to heed anyone. The expression may criticise defiance; it does not require obedience to every demand.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source supplies an idiomatic gloss, not a religious incident.

entry_comparison_index.title: Coincidence is not cause
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Two events occurring together can be mistaken for cause and effect. The crow’s call and the falling fruit provide a compact warning against that leap.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Farming in boastful talk
entry_comparison_index.meaning: In this source’s gloss, the expression mocks undertaking or talking about work without understanding it. The element Barabati is retained untranslated and is not independently resolved here.
entry_comparison_index.context: No origin story is supplied. The wording alone does not establish a place or an actual farming episode.

entry_comparison_index.title: An impossible demand
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image turns coercion into an absurd demand: an oath cannot make an impossible task reasonable. The source gloss concerns forcing someone to act.
entry_comparison_index.context: Dheṅki is a large husking implement; swallowing it is hyperbole, not an action to imitate.

entry_comparison_index.title: Planning an impossible meal
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source uses ingredients brought together in an impossible way to mock an unrealistic proposition. Chilika supplies an image in the saying, not proof of where it originated.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Anger at someone’s very presence
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source explains this as intense anger towards someone. Avoiding even their shadow exaggerates how complete that rejection feels.
entry_comparison_index.context: An emotional exaggeration, not a claim about shadows.

entry_comparison_index.title: Disrupting the gathering
entry_comparison_index.meaning: An orderly gathering is disturbed without need. The animal image conveys the disruption; no real release of an animal is implied.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Trouble from within
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source gloss points to a breach of trust from someone relied upon. The damage comes from within the thing meant to work properly.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Recognising quality
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Experience can help a person recognise quality that others miss. This is a craft metaphor, not an inherited ability or a claim about every member of a community.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Finding what was needed
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source applies this to finding something needed unexpectedly. The pleasure lies in the search meeting its object.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Words without substance
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Food lacking salt becomes an image for talk that has little substance. It questions what the words contribute, not a person’s manner of speaking.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Describing what one has never seen
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source mocks confident description without firsthand knowledge. The stated number belongs to the boast being questioned, not a botanical lesson.
entry_comparison_index.context: No claim about the fruit’s actual structure.

entry_comparison_index.title: A precious gift without appreciation
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source presents a valuable gift going to someone unable to appreciate it. Used of people, the comparison can insult; it should not be treated as a judgment of anyone’s inherent worth.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Blaming the road
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A person shifts responsibility for their own mistake onto the circumstances. The saying asks whether the difficulty really lies outside them.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Pride before a fall
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source invokes Ravana’s downfall as an image of destructive pride. It warns against arrogance through a literary-religious allusion, not a verified historical event.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Hope for the unprotected
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The saying expresses faith that someone without protection may still find help. It offers reassurance, not a reason to withhold practical assistance.
entry_comparison_index.context: A statement of faith, not a guaranteed outcome.

entry_comparison_index.title: The danger of knowing only a little
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A partial understanding can cause trouble when someone acts as if it were enough. The warning is against misplaced certainty, not against beginning to learn.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: How we meet the world
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source reads this as a reminder that our conduct can influence how others respond. It is not proof that mistreatment is always the victim’s fault.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Good words from an unexpected mouth
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The contrast expresses surprise at hearing something good from someone associated with the opposite. The mythological names sharpen the irony.
entry_comparison_index.context: No particular scriptural episode or historical origin is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.title: Darkness beneath the lamp
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source applies the image to someone who attends to others while neglecting those close by. Light reaching outward does not mean every nearby place receives it.
entry_comparison_index.context: The recorded wording is explained here without assigning an inventor, date or place of origin.

entry_comparison_index.title: Caught in a sticky predicament
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source explains the expression as getting into severe difficulty. The image conveys being caught and unable to move freely.
entry_comparison_index.context: No particular trapping implement or historical origin is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଅଇଲା ମାଳି, ମାଇଲା ତାଳି
ଧରି ପଳେଇଲା, ଖେଚୁଡ଼ି ଥାଳି।
entry_comparison_index.title: A distraction and a stolen meal
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A show of activity diverts attention while someone takes the thing that matters. The rhyme exposes the trick rather than admiring the theft.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source supplies a deception gloss. ମାଳି is retained as the rhyme’s label; it is not evidence about a community’s conduct.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଅଗସ୍ତି ଦେଲେ ଦାନ
କଷା ଗୁଆକୁ ପଚା ପାନ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: A gift with little to give
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The announcement of generosity is undercut by the poor gift itself. This is an editorial reading of the contrast; the rhyme does not establish a historical donor or event.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source gives no explanatory gloss. Agasti is not identified here with a verified person; no antiquity claim follows from the name.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଅଗା, ବଗା, ଖଗା
ତିନିହେଁ ତିନି ଅଲଗା ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Three people, three ways
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Being grouped together does not make people alike. The little series of names makes difference easy to remember; the particular disagreement depends on the occasion.
entry_comparison_index.context: A literal, bounded editorial reading; the source supplies no origin story or named real individuals.

entry_comparison_index.title: Running after every chance
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source uses this comparison for someone rushing about in pursuit of money. It can criticise restless chasing, but it is a dismissive expression rather than a neutral description of a person.
entry_comparison_index.context: The captured example supplies the money-seeking situation. This is an animal comparison, not a statement about human worth.

entry_comparison_index.title: Standing like a post
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Someone remains standing stiffly or motionlessly. In the source’s example, the speaker has already invited the person to sit; the comparison conveys impatience, not a diagnosis of the person’s motives.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source’s invitation-to-sit example supports this limited reading; no claim of laziness or incapacity is warranted.

entry_comparison_index.title: Good intentions, a spoiled result
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The intended improvement turns into a spoiled result. Good intentions alone do not guarantee that the work will turn out as planned.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source provides an explicit spoiled-work gloss and a synonymous expression. The image is not evidence of an actual sculptor or religious episode.

entry_comparison_index.title: A benefit out of reach
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A desirable thing can become available without helping someone who cannot make use of it. The saying asks who actually benefits, not merely whether something is good.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source gloss concerns a useful thing failing to reach the appropriate person. The fruit-and-crow image is proverbial, not a biological claim about every crow.

entry_comparison_index.title: Neglect shows in the result
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A small task left undone leaves a visible result. The source extends the image to work stalled through lack of effort; it does not make every unfinished task a moral failure.
entry_comparison_index.context: The moustache is the domestic image in the wording, not a rule about gender or proper appearance.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଅରଣା ମଇଁଷି ରହିଛି ଅନାଇ, ମଇଁଷିର ପାଖ ନଯାଅ ଦନାଇ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Keep clear of a known danger
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The warning makes caution concrete: noticing a danger should change how close one goes to it. This is a bounded editorial reading of the warning, not a documented account of an encounter.
entry_comparison_index.context: ଦନାଇ occurs as an address in the line. The source gives no biographical evidence or authorship proof for this name.

entry_comparison_index.title: An old habit returns
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source uses the curved tail as an image of a persistent disposition. In ordinary conversation it can express frustration when a habit returns; it does not prove that people are incapable of change.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source’s fixed-nature gloss is reported as a proverbial attitude, not endorsed as psychology or a judgment on a whole group.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ବିରି ମାଡ଼ ଶୁଣି କୋଳଥ ଚୋପା
ହରଡ଼ କହୁଛି ରଖଲୋ ବାପା ॥
entry_comparison_index.title: Frightened by another’s trouble
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source explains the fear that spreads when someone sees another in trouble. The pulses speak as if the next blow might reach them too.
entry_comparison_index.context: The first clause is elliptical in the captured wording. It is preserved without supplying a missing verb; the source gloss supports the shared-fear reading.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଉପର ବରଡ଼ା ଖସୁଛି,
ମଝି ବରଡ଼ା ହସୁଛି 
ତଳ ବରଡ଼ା କହୁଛି,
ମୋ ଦିନ କାଳ ଯାଉଛିରେ ଭାଇ ତୋ ଦିନକାଳ ଆସୁଛି ॥
entry_comparison_index.title: Do not laugh at another’s turn
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaking leaves place laughter beside the passing of time. Read cautiously, the verse warns against treating another’s decline as something that can never reach oneself.
entry_comparison_index.context: No explanatory gloss accompanies this verse. The sequence of upper, middle and lower leaves is retained exactly; no botanical species, original voice or corrected sequence is asserted.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ବେଙ୍ଗ କହେ ବେଙ୍ଗୁଲିଲୋ ପୃଥ୍ଵୀ ଘଡ଼ିକେ ଆନ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: The world keeps changing
entry_comparison_index.meaning: Circumstances do not remain as they were. The animal conversation makes a simple observation about change, without saying that every change is good or bad.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source explicitly glosses changing circumstances; the dialogue is not attached to a verified folktale here.

entry_comparison_index.title: Distance does not end a claim
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The line presents a claim that persists despite distance. Applied figuratively, it can suggest that being out of sight does not by itself remove someone’s connection or responsibility.
entry_comparison_index.context: No source gloss accompanies the line. It is not used as evidence for any historical law giving a king ownership of all elephants.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଉପକାର କଲି କୁକୁରକୁ କୁକୁର ମୁତିଲା ଉପରକୁ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Help answered with an insult
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The crude image expresses resentment when help is answered with harm or disrespect. It describes a feeling of betrayal, not a reason to assume everyone who needs help will be ungrateful.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source gives an ingratitude gloss. The bodily image is intentionally coarse and should not be presented as polite praise or animal-behaviour evidence.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଠକ ଠକ ମାଳି ଭଜନ ଟାଣ
ଭୋକ କଲା ଭାତ ପାଖକୁ ଆଣ |
entry_comparison_index.title: Devotion and an empty stomach
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse sets a loud display of devotion beside an ordinary appetite. It can be read as a jab at performance that conceals self-interest, though the source gives no separate explanation.
entry_comparison_index.context: ମାଳି remains a source label, not a judgment about a caste or occupation. Neither hunger nor devotional singing is itself treated as proof of hypocrisy. The opening ଠକ ଠକ and ଭଜନ ଟାଣ are not given a definite literal gloss; the interpretation remains provisional.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଆତଙ୍କ ବେଳେ ଯାଚନ୍ତି କୁକୁଡ଼ା, ଆତଙ୍କ ଗଲେ ଦିଅନ୍ତି ନେଫେଡ଼ା
entry_comparison_index.title: Promises made in a crisis
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source explains this as a vow made to God during danger and neglected once the danger passes. More broadly, it can remind someone not to forget a promise after receiving help. The precise meaning of the final noun is unresolved; the interpretation follows the supplied gloss.
entry_comparison_index.context: The religious vow is the source’s explanatory setting, not a recommendation or a claim that everyone follows this practice. A previously deferred dictionary saying has different wording; no equivalence or repaired final word is certified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ମାଲୁଣି ହାତରେ ଲଙ୍କା ମରିଚଲୋ, ମାଳି ହାତେ ଫୁଲ ହାର, ଯାହା ମନ କଥା, ସିଏ ଜାଣେ ସିନା, ତାହା କି ଜାଣିବ ପର ॥
entry_comparison_index.title: Only you know what is in your heart
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The closing lines remind us that another person’s private thoughts are not directly visible. The everyday objects lead into that contrast; this reading does not assign a hidden moral meaning to the chillies or garland. Ask rather than assume what someone feels.
entry_comparison_index.context: Listed as a saying in this community anthology; author, earliest use and possible song or literary relationships remain unverified. Gardener words are translated as occupational imagery, not evidence about any community’s traits.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଆହାରେ ଭଲ ମନ୍ଦ ନାହିଁ,
 ଯେ ସ୍ଥାନେ ଯେବଣ ମିଳଇ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Contentment with what comes
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse sets aside distinctions between preferred and less preferred food: one accepts what is available. A related passage in Jagannath Das’s Odia Bhagabata places this thought in the Avadhuta’s account to King Yadu of equanimity and the python as a teacher. Read in everyday conversation, it can counsel contentment instead of constant complaint. That everyday application is an interpretation, not an account of the saying’s first use.
entry_comparison_index.context: The related Bhagabata text is an ascetic teaching about contentment. Its chapter 9, verse 5 reads ଯେମନ୍ତ where the selected Incubator witness reads ଯେବଣ; keep both readings distinct. Neither this comparison nor the modern compilation establishes a first coinage or a direction of borrowing.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ବିଦ୍ୟା ଅଟଇ ମହାଧନ 
ବାଳକେ କର ଉପାର୍ଜନ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Learning as wealth
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse calls learning wealth and directly addresses children. Unlike a possession handed over once, learning must be acquired through effort. The comparison gives everyday study a value beyond an immediate reward; it does not promise that education alone removes every hardship.
entry_comparison_index.context: The direct address to children and paired lines make this a didactic verse. The captured compilation places it under instructive Dhaga but supplies no author or literary work; attribution must remain unresolved.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ବୈକୁଣ୍ଠ ସମାନ ଆହା ଅଟେ ସେହି ଘର, 
 ପରସ୍ପର ସ୍ନେହ ଯହିଁ ଥାଏ ନିରନ୍ତର ।
entry_comparison_index.title: A home held together by affection
