entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse imagines an ideal home through the affection people show one another. The important word is mutual: care is not demanded from just one person. Its heavenly comparison celebrates a quality of relationships rather than the size or expense of a house.
entry_comparison_index.context: Vaikuntha supplies the religious comparison. This is an ideal expressed in verse, not evidence about every household or a reason to remain in a harmful relationship. No original author or work is identified by the captured entry.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ମର୍ତ୍ୟ ମଣ୍ଡଳେ ଦେହ ବହି
ଦେବତା ହୋଇଲେ ମରଇ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: No embodied life is beyond death
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse uses the strongest possible contrast: even divinity does not escape death after taking bodily form in the mortal world. Read as counsel, it asks the listener to recognise the limits of embodied life. Its force is reflective and religious, not a factual account of a particular death.
entry_comparison_index.context: The wording resembles a literary or devotional maxim; the saved compilation alone does not establish its original work or oral circulation. Do not present it as medical advice or use it to dismiss someone’s grief.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଯେ ପାଞ୍ଚେ ପର ର ମନ୍ଦ
ତା ମନ୍ଦ ପାଞ୍ଚନ୍ତି ଗୋବିନ୍ଦ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Ill will turned back on its maker
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse warns against deliberately wishing or planning another person’s misfortune. It imagines that ill will being answered by Govinda. This is a religious moral warning, not a guarantee that every wrongdoer will suffer or that a person’s suffering proves wrongdoing.
entry_comparison_index.context: Govinda is retained as the named divine figure in the source. The compilation supplies no separate explanation or attribution. The moral should not be converted into victim-blaming or a prediction of supernatural punishment.

entry_comparison_index.title: Persistence meets resistance
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The same word changes force across the line: the iron resists, while the smith refuses to give up. The dictionary explicitly marks these two senses. The image suggests meeting a difficult task with sustained effort rather than expecting it to yield immediately. It need not turn persistence into an obligation to continue every losing effort.
entry_comparison_index.context: The craft image concerns resistance and effort; it does not describe an inherited trait of a community. Parenthetical dictionary sense numbers are omitted from the displayed wording and recorded as an editorial change.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଚଇତା ! ତବତ ଖାଇବୁ କି ପଖାଳ ଖାଇବୁ ବେଳ ଥାଉଁ ଥାଉଁ କହିଥା
entry_comparison_index.title: Say what you want in time
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The pointed address and choice between hot food and pakhala turn a practical request into a memorable line: say what you want while another person still has time to arrange it. The dictionary marks Chaita as a non-respectful form of Chaitanya, so the tone can carry impatience or a dismissive edge. Applying it to other decisions is an editorial reading of the complete quoted example; its first occasion is unknown.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source identifies Chaita as a non-respectful or dismissive form of Chaitanya. No particular historical person or household is established. Pakhala remains a named food; the wording should not be softened into a uniformly polite request.

entry_comparison_index.title: Care for the person doing the work
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The dictionary places this saying under caring for the body and health. Duty does not erase the needs of the person who performs it. In a wider everyday application, commitment and care for oneself can belong together; exhaustion is not the only measure of sincerity.
entry_comparison_index.context: The religious wording is preserved. The broader work example is new editorial application, not a medical recommendation or a rule attributed to a particular ritual.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ନାଚିଲା ଲୋକକୁ ଲାଜ ନାହିଁ ଦେଖିଲା ଲୋକକୁ ଲାଜ
entry_comparison_index.title: Embarrassed on someone else’s behalf
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The dictionary explains a mismatch: someone behaves without embarrassment while witnesses feel ashamed on that person’s behalf. The saying can name that uncomfortable distance between an action and how it appears to others. Its image need not be used to condemn dancing or to police someone’s harmless enjoyment.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary explicitly labels the entry a proverb and gives this social-use gloss. Its alternative scatological wording is not needed for this candidate.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ବାର ହାତ କାକୁଡ଼ିର ତେର ହାତ ମଞ୍ଜି
entry_comparison_index.title: A seed bigger than its fruit
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The part has become larger than the whole that supposedly contains it. The dictionary explicitly calls this an impossible claim. The absurd measurements make a quick test for an exaggerated story: do its own details fit together? The point is inconsistency, not an accurate description of cucumber growth.
entry_comparison_index.context: Traditional hand-based length language is translated as cubits without a modern centimetre conversion. The source also records a sheath/sword variant, not a separate entry.

entry_comparison_index.title: A boat needs a river
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A useful boat cannot replace the water it needs. The image invites a distinction between ability and the conditions that make ability useful. When an essential resource disappears, blaming the tool or the person alone may miss the real obstacle. This wider application is an editorial interpretation of the quoted saying.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source supplies the complete example under a river drying up, but no historical origin or detailed figurative-use account. Similar dependency themes elsewhere in the collection do not make this wording an exact duplicate.

entry_comparison_index.title: When spending outgrows income
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The dictionary explicitly applies this architectural comparison to expenditure exceeding income. What should be a supporting part has grown beyond the thing that supports it. The image asks us to notice proportion in a plan, especially when its surrounding costs threaten to consume more than the available means.
entry_comparison_index.context: The comparison follows the source’s figurative explanation; it does not establish a universal architectural rule or identify a particular temple. The unusual source spelling ବିଳିଯିବା remains unchanged.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଅପାଇ ପାଇଚି ପିଲା,
ନା ଗାଁ ଯାକ କିଲିବିଲା...!!!
entry_comparison_index.title: A whole village stirred by one household
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A private event becomes everybody’s noisy business. The source introduces this saying as something used when someone makes too much of a display. Its joke lies in the size of the response: one household’s news seems to shake an entire village.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source explicitly supplies a display/show-off context. Apai is retained as an unidentified source designation; no historical person, kinship role or gender is inferred. The criticism is of disproportionate display, not of celebrating a child.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଚୂଲିମୂଳେ ନହୁଣିଆ ପାରୁଥିବ ବିଲେଇ...
ପୁଅ ଦେଖଉଚି ନୁଖୁରା ବଡ଼େଇ...!!
entry_comparison_index.title: Boasting beside the kitchen stove
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source introduces this line for unnecessary swagger. A cat’s ordinary-looking movement by the stove is set beside a boy making much of himself. The disproportion makes the boast look small: loud self-display is not itself an achievement.
entry_comparison_index.context: The dictionary lists nahunia as a kind of bodily exercise, which supports retaining an exercise image; no precise pose or movement sequence is established. The source’s own usage condition supports the swagger reading. The literal rendering of ନୁଖୁରା as empty remains contextual rather than separately dictionary-certified.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ବୁଡ଼ି କରି ପାଣି ପିଇଲେ ମହାଦେବଙ୍କ ବାପା ମଧ୍ୟ ଜାଣି ପରିବେ ନାହିଁ
entry_comparison_index.title: A secret concealed inside an ordinary action
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The dictionary places this example under doing something secretly. Drinking is hidden within the larger act of being underwater, so an observer cannot easily separate one from the other. The extravagant appeal to Mahadev’s father makes the claim of secrecy comic. It can describe someone’s confidence that a concealed action will escape notice; it does not establish that deception always succeeds.
entry_comparison_index.context: The expression is comic hyperbole, not theological genealogy or an instruction to drink underwater. Source spelling ପରିବେ is retained, not silently changed to ପାରିବେ.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ପୁତୁରା ସାଙ୍ଗରେ କଳି କଲି, ମହୁର ତିଅଣରୁ ମେଞ୍ଚାଏ ପାଆନ୍ତି, ତୁଣ୍ଡ ପରସାଦୁଁ ନାଶ ଗଲି
entry_comparison_index.title: Talking oneself out of a welcome meal
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The speaker looks back on a quarrel and the food they might otherwise have enjoyed. The dictionary defines ମେଞ୍ଚାଏ as a large portion of food. Here the humorous self-accusation turns an abstract consequence of quarrelling into a lost meal: the mouth that wanted food also said the words that cost it. This is a close reading of the example, not a reconstructed family incident.
entry_comparison_index.context: Mahura is retained as a named curry; no ingredients, temple recipe or historical household are inferred. The reading concerns needless quarrelling, not an obligation to remain silent about mistreatment.

entry_comparison_index.odia: କାମ ପଡ଼ିଲେ କାଜି, କାମ ଛାଡ଼ିଲେ ପାଜି
entry_comparison_index.title: Respect that lasts only while help is needed
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The paired words move abruptly from a title of authority to an insult. Read together, they expose respect that depends entirely on another person’s usefulness: someone is important while needed and dismissed afterward. The target of this reading is the speaker’s opportunism, not the integrity of qazis or any religious community.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source defines qazi as a Muslim judge and explicitly labels the paired line ଢଗ; a separate lexical entry confirms ପାଜି is an insult. Institutional history in the old dictionary is not adopted as present-day law or status.

entry_comparison_index.title: A lesson that stays with you
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The praise has an ironic edge. The source explains the expression as remembering someone after receiving a hard lesson from them. The repeated work of washing the sack makes that memory linger: the consequences remain after the encounter is over. It can be a rueful comment on having been taken in, rather than sincere gratitude.
entry_comparison_index.context: The source supplies the hard-lesson gloss but no story explaining why a sack is washed. The sack image and ironic praise are retained without inventing that missing story.

entry_comparison_index.title: Nothing left at the root
entry_comparison_index.meaning: This is an expression for complete destruction, not merely a setback or a surface change. The source pairs it with another expression and explicitly glosses both as destroying something entirely. The root image makes the degree of loss clear: what might have allowed it to continue has also been removed.
entry_comparison_index.context: Selected as the second expression in the source’s slash-separated pair ଖୋଳ କରିବା/ମୂଳପୋଛ କରିବା. The source’s first term is retained as a related expression, not silently translated through a guessed literal sense or counted as a second entry.

entry_comparison_index.title: The tether and the horse
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The source applies this image to disorder under weak supervision. The horse’s movement is viewed in relation to what holds it, so the remark turns attention from the actor alone to the arrangement around them. In a wider everyday application, repeated disorder may reveal that responsibilities or boundaries have not been made clear. That wider application is editorial; the source does not supply a history of the image.
entry_comparison_index.context: The weak-supervision reading comes from this source’s gloss. Other readings of strength or support are not established here. The comparison is not a recommendation for harsh discipline or a claim that people are animals.

entry_comparison_index.title: The words will outlast the moment
entry_comparison_index.meaning: A conversation ends, but what was said can remain in memory. The dictionary labels this short line a Dhaga under “for ever”. It can give a promise weight or warn that a remark will not be easily forgotten. Which feeling it carries depends on the speaker and the occasion; the source does not specify a single original scene.
entry_comparison_index.context: Possible uses are editorial readings, not recorded testimony. Source spelling ରହିୟିବ is retained; no guarantee that every utterance survives.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ତୋର ମୋର ରାଜି, କିସ କରିବ କାଜି
entry_comparison_index.title: When both of us agree
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The rhyme between raji and qazi turns agreement into a cheeky challenge to an outside authority. The dictionary places it under the qazi’s marriage-registration role. Its force is rhetorical: if the people concerned agree, why should someone else obstruct them? That is the speaker’s claim, not a statement that consent removes legal duties.
entry_comparison_index.context: Preserve the named role without religious caricature. Surrounding dictionary institutional claims are not adopted as present law or independently verified history.

entry_comparison_index.title: Land to cultivate, yet no meal
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The joke places a substantial-looking agricultural resource beside an empty stomach. The source explains it as plenty of rice but too little cooked food. Possession and actual provision have come apart: what looks sufficient has not become something usable. The saying does not identify one universal cause for that mismatch.
entry_comparison_index.context: Bati is retained as the source’s land-measure term; no regional conversion is supplied. The witness spells the daily expression ନୀତି, which is preserved. The accompanying gloss, not an invented household story, supports the reading.

entry_comparison_index.odia:
ଧୀର ସ୍ଥିର ନୋହି ଉତ୍ତେଜିତ ହେଲେ
କାର୍ଯ୍ୟ କେବେ ସିଦ୍ଧ ନୁହେଁ ।
ଧୀରପାଣି ସିନା ପଥର କାଟଇ
ସ୍ରୋତ ତହିଁ ବ୍ୟର୍ଥ ହୁଏ  ॥
entry_comparison_index.title: Quiet persistence against a rush
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The verse gives patient work the quieter but stronger image. Water that keeps returning to the stone stands against a rush of agitation. Its supplied gloss recommends thinking and acting steadily instead of becoming angry. The absolute contrast belongs to the verse’s exhortation; it is not a scientific claim that fast water cannot erode stone.
entry_comparison_index.context: This four-line exhortation appears in the collection of traditional sayings, with a supplied gloss. No named poet, composition date, tune or independent evidence of proverbial circulation is established in this pass. Its four-line form is retained, not silently shortened to a slogan.

entry_comparison_index.title: Staying alive to carry something forward
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The short line makes survival the condition for carrying a family name forward. The collection’s gloss extends the thought towards being able to help the world by first getting oneself ahead. This is a reminder that continuing to live and act matters; it does not establish that another person’s welfare is unimportant.
entry_comparison_index.context: The father’s name is the source’s family image, not a claim that only sons sustain families. English “lives on” supplies the implied continuation rather than an additional historical assertion. No origin story is supplied.

entry_comparison_index.odia: ଜାଣି ଘୋଡ଼ାର ଶିଙ୍ଗ ନାହିଁ, ଶିଙ୍ଗ ଥିଲେ ଘୋଡ଼ା ରଖନ୍ତା ନାହିଁ ।
entry_comparison_index.title: Imagine a horse with horns
entry_comparison_index.meaning: The image starts with an already powerful animal and imagines giving it another weapon. The collection explains the line as a limit on the strength granted to the strong: with still more power, they might heed nobody. The humour is in the impossible extra equipment, not in a claim that real horses are naturally malicious.
entry_comparison_index.context: The supplied gloss invokes divine restraint; this is the collection’s explanation, not evidence for a particular myth or author. The last clause’s omitted object is rendered “no one” in English in line with the gloss’s reference to heeding nobody. The opening ଜାଣି does not securely establish who knows or intends this; the English does not turn it into an imperative. Its agency remains unresolved.

Source-specific gloss versus editorial literal/meaning/application; full bilingual fields and no unsupported origins.
Semantic distinctness beyond string matching, including185 entries and earlier related/deferred dispositions.
